statement: The central limit theorem does not apply to extreme losses, because extremes are not described by the normal limit of averages.
explanation: The central limit theorem concerns averages, whereas extremes are governed by different limit laws, so the CLT does not describe them.
originalText: The central limit theorem (CLT) does not apply.

statement: Extreme value theory estimates are subject to considerable model risk.
explanation: Tail estimates are fitted from few observations and are highly sensitive to the chosen model and its parameters.
originalText: EVT estimates are subject to considerable model risk.

statement: Extreme value theory cannot, by definition, provide loss estimates beyond the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.
explanation: EVT fits a parametric tail model and extrapolates beyond the sample maximum, so its loss estimates are not capped at the worst observed loss.
originalText: EVT cannot, by definition, provide loss estimates beyond (in excess of) the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.
correction: Extreme value theory can provide loss estimates beyond the worst actual observed loss in the historical sample.

changes.to: can provide

statement: Extreme value theory is inherently difficult because the sample contains few relevant loss observations.
explanation: Extreme losses are rare by definition, so the scarcity of tail observations is the core difficulty of EVT.
originalText: EVT is inherently difficult because our sample contains few relevant loss observations.

statement: Extreme events tend to recur at rather regular time intervals.
explanation: Extreme events are rare and irregular; they are taken seriously because they are very costly, not because they recur on a schedule.
correction: Extreme events do not tend to recur at regular time intervals.

changes.from: tend to recur at rather regular
changes.to: do not tend to recur at regular

statement: Extreme events rarely have warning signs, so markets cannot prepare for them in any way.
explanation: This overstates the case: markets can prepare for extreme events using tools such as stress testing and extreme value theory.
originalText: Extreme events rarely have warning signs and thus markets cannot prepare for them in any way.

statement: Extreme events, although rare, are taken seriously in finance because they are normally very costly and can create a ripple effect on the global market.
explanation: Extreme events have a low probability but a huge loss when they occur, and the losses can cascade through the system, so they must be identified and managed.
originalText: Extreme events are normally very costly and can create a ripple effect on the global market.

statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is modelling the tail dependence structure among extreme values using extreme value copulas.
explanation: Univariate EVT already handles each marginal tail; what the multivariate extension adds is the joint behaviour of extremes, captured by tail dependence through EV copulas.
originalText: Modeling the tail dependence structure among the extreme values, using extreme value copulas

statement: Multivariate extreme value theory fits a separate generalized Pareto distribution to each risk factor and ignores joint behaviour.
explanation: Fitting each factor separately is univariate EVT; the point of the multivariate extension is to model the tail dependence between the factors.
originalText: Fitting a separate generalized Pareto distribution to each risk factor and ignoring joint behavior

statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is estimating the pairwise linear correlation matrix under an elliptical distribution.
explanation: Linear correlation and elliptical assumptions capture tail dependence poorly; multivariate EVT instead models tail dependence with extreme value copulas.
originalText: Estimating the pairwise linear correlation matrix under an elliptical distribution

statement: The central focus of multivariate extreme value theory is calibrating the central limit theorem to the sample means of the risk factors.
explanation: The CLT describes the distribution of averages, whereas EVT concerns the tails, so it is the wrong tool for extremes.
originalText: Calibrating the central limit theorem to the sample means of the risk factors

statement: As the number of random variables increases, multivariate extreme value theory suffers from a curse of dimensionality.
explanation: Adding variables makes joint extreme observations rarer and the number of parameters larger.
originalText: As the number of random variables increases, multivariate EVT suffers from a ”curse of dimensionality”

statement: Multivariate extreme value dependence can be modelled by assuming an extreme value copula.
explanation: The limiting distribution of multivariate extremes belongs to the extreme value copula family, so dependence is modelled by assuming one.
originalText: We can model multivariate extreme value dependence by assuming an EV copula

statement: In multivariate extreme value theory, extreme events can generally be assumed to be independent.
explanation: The rationale for multivariate EVT is that extremes are typically dependent (tail dependence, for example a disaster hitting many markets), so independence cannot generally be assumed.
originalText: We can generally assume that extreme events are independent
correction: In multivariate extreme value theory, extreme events cannot generally be assumed to be independent.

changes.from: can generally be assumed to be independent
changes.to: cannot generally be assumed to be independent

statement: In multivariate extreme value theory, as dimensionality increases there are fewer multivariate extreme observations but more parameters to estimate.
explanation: Joint extremes become very scarce (for example about 1 in 10,000 for two variables each extreme 1 time in 100) while the number of parameters grows.
originalText: As dimensionality increases, there are fewer multivariate extreme observations but more parameters to estimate

statement: A VaR model at 99% confidence is consistent with accuracy when its exception rate is close to 1%, for example about 5 exceptions over 500 trading days.
explanation: An accurate model produces exceptions at a rate equal to 1 minus the confidence level, apart from sampling variation.
originalText: About 5 exceptions, so that the exception rate is close to 1%

statement: About 25 exceptions over 500 trading days, a 5% exception rate, is consistent with an accurate 99% one-day VaR model.
explanation: A 5% exception rate is what a 95% VaR should produce; at 99% confidence it would show that the model understates risk.
originalText: About 25 exceptions, so that the exception rate is close to 5%

statement: A VaR backtest should show zero exceptions, since a loss should never exceed VaR.
explanation: Zero exceptions is not the goal: too few exceptions signals an overly conservative model that overstates risk and ties up capital.
originalText: Zero exceptions, since a loss should never exceed VaR

statement: In a VaR backtest the number of exceptions is irrelevant if the average daily loss is below VaR.
explanation: Backtesting looks at the frequency of losses beyond VaR, not at the average loss, so the exception count is the key test statistic.
originalText: The number of exceptions is irrelevant if the average daily loss is below VaR

statement: A VaR backtest works the same way for any VaR method: daily VaR is compared with the realized P&L and the exceptions are counted against the expected number, such as 2.5 over 250 days at 99% confidence.
explanation: The backtest depends only on the stated confidence level and the realized outcomes, so it is independent of the method used to compute VaR.
originalText: It works the same for any VaR method: daily VaR is compared with the realized P&L and the exceptions counted against the expected 2.5

statement: A VaR backtest is only meaningful if VaR is computed with the parametric (delta-normal) method.
explanation: Parametric VaR gets no special treatment in a backtest; the exceptions are counted and compared with the expected number whatever the method.
originalText: It is only meaningful if VaR is computed with the parametric (delta‑normal) method

statement: Backtesting is easier with historical simulation VaR because the VaR is based on actual returns.
explanation: Historical simulation VaR is no more testable than other methods; using actual past returns does not change the exception count or the expected frequency.
originalText: It is easier with historical simulation because the VaR is based on actual returns

statement: A VaR backtest requires Monte Carlo VaR because only then can the expected number of exceptions be derived.
explanation: The expected number of exceptions comes from the confidence level (for example 250 x 1% = 2.5), not from simulation.
originalText: It requires Monte Carlo VaR because only then can the expected number of exceptions be derived

statement: Backtesting compares VaR forecasts with subsequently realized profits and losses.
explanation: This is the definition of VaR backtesting.
originalText: Backtesting compares VaR forecasts with subsequently realized profits and losses

statement: A significantly higher number of exceptions than expected suggests that a VaR model understates risk.
explanation: Excess exceptions mean losses exceeded VaR too often, so the model underestimates risk.
originalText: A significantly higher number of exceptions than expected suggests the model understates risk

statement: Under the Basel internal models approach, banks must backtest their VaR models.
explanation: Basel requires backtesting, with a higher capital multiplier applied when there are too many exceptions.
originalText: Under the Basel internal models approach, banks must backtest their VaR models

statement: A VaR model with zero exceptions over a long sample is necessarily the most accurate.
explanation: Accuracy means exceptions occur at the expected rate; zero exceptions over a long sample points to an overly conservative model that overstates risk.
originalText: A model with zero exceptions over a long sample is necessarily the most accurate
correction: A VaR model with zero exceptions over a long sample is not necessarily the most accurate.

changes.to: is not necessarily the most accurate

statement: When a VaR model produces more exceptions than forecast, it understates risk, so the risk-taking units of the bank are likely to be allocated less capital than they should be.
explanation: Too many exceptions mean VaR is too low, and capital allocated on the basis of that VaR is therefore too low.
originalText: The risk‑taking units of the bank will likely be allocated less capital than they should be.

statement: A VaR model that produces more exceptions than forecast is most likely overestimating the market risk faced by the bank.
explanation: Overestimation would produce fewer exceptions than forecast; more exceptions than forecast indicate that risk is underestimated.
originalText: The model is most likely overestimating the market risk faced by the bank.
correction: A VaR model that produces more exceptions than forecast is most likely underestimating the market risk faced by the bank.

changes.to: underestimating

statement: Employing Monte Carlo simulated p-values instead of asymptotic distributions addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting and gives a correctly sized test.
explanation: Simulating the test statistic's null distribution at the actual sample size replaces the unreliable large-sample approximation.
originalText: Employing Monte Carlo simulated p‑values instead of relying on asymptotic distributions.

statement: Using asymptotic (chi-squared) distributions for p-value calculation addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting.
explanation: The asymptotic chi-squared approximation is the source of the poor test size when exceptions are few, not the cure for it.
originalText: Using asymptotic (chi‑squared) distributions for p‑value calculation.

statement: Increasing the VaR confidence level, for example from 99% to 99.9%, addresses the small-sample problem in VaR backtesting.
explanation: A higher confidence level lowers the expected number of exceptions (for example 250 x 0.001 = 0.25), which worsens the small-sample problem.
originalText: Increasing the VaR confidence level (e.g., from 99% to 99.9%).

statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting can mask actual portfolio losses and make the VaR model appear more accurate than it is.
explanation: Such non-risk revenue is typically positive and offsets trading losses, so fewer exceptions are recorded than the model actually deserves.
originalText: It could have masked actual portfolio losses, making the VaR model appear more accurate than it was.

statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting leads to an underestimation of VaR and insufficient capital reserves.
explanation: The contamination affects the P&L series used in the backtest, not the VaR estimate itself, which is not computed from these items.
originalText: It could have led to an underestimation of VaR, resulting in insufficient capital reserves.

statement: Including fees, commissions and intraday trading revenue in the P&L used for VaR backtesting significantly increases the computational complexity of VaR calculations.
explanation: The VaR calculation is unchanged; only the P&L series it is compared with is affected.
originalText: It increased the computational complexity of VaR calculations significantly.

statement: A VaR model that fails a backtest on hypothetical returns indicates that the VaR modelling methodology itself must be adjusted, because VaR assumes a static portfolio.
explanation: Hypothetical returns isolate the model's own assumption of a constant portfolio from non-modelled P&L effects such as intraday trading and fees.
originalText: Hypothetical returns

statement: VaR backtesting should use both actual returns, the total return on the trading portfolio, and hypothetical returns, the returns obtained by freezing the starting positions.
explanation: Backtesting both series separates model error (hypothetical returns fail) from intraday trading and fee effects (only actual returns fail).
originalText: The actual returns, which correspond to the total return on the bank’s trading portfolio, and the hypothetical returns, which represent the returns obtained from freezing the starting positions in the bank’s trading portfolio

statement: VaR mapping replaces the current values of many positions with exposures to a smaller set of selected primitive risk factors, because modelling each position separately is impractical.
explanation: Mapping aggregates many positions into exposures on a limited set of primitive risk factors, which simplifies risk measurement.
originalText: The current values of many positions are replaced by exposures to a smaller set of selected primitive risk factors, because modeling each position separately is impractical.

statement: In VaR mapping, only the most extreme (abnormal) risk factors are retained, because normal factors do not contribute to tail losses.
explanation: Mapping covers the factors that drive the portfolio's risk; it does not filter down to only abnormal factors.
originalText: Only the most extreme (abnormal) risk factors are retained, because normal factors do not contribute to tail losses.

statement: In VaR mapping, each position is mapped to every risk factor that could affect its price, so that no approximation error is introduced.
explanation: Using every factor would defeat the simplifying purpose of mapping, which deliberately accepts some approximation.
originalText: Each position is mapped to every risk factor that could affect its price, so that no approximation error is introduced.

statement: In VaR mapping, every portfolio is mapped to exactly five risk factors regardless of its composition.
explanation: The number of risk factors is chosen to fit the portfolio, as a trade-off between accuracy and speed; five is arbitrary.
originalText: Every portfolio is mapped to exactly five risk factors regardless of its composition.

statement: VaR mapping is especially useful for instruments whose characteristics change over time, such as a fixed-rate bond whose maturity and interest rate sensitivity shrink as it ages, or an option whose sensitivity to the underlying changes with the market.
explanation: Past prices of such instruments misstate their current risk, so they are mapped to risk factors that reflect their current profile.
originalText: A fixed‑rate bond whose maturity and interest rate sensitivity shrink as it ages, or an option whose sensitivity to the underlying changes with the market.

statement: If a position's exposures to its risk factors sum to less than its market value and no relevant risk factor has been omitted, the remainder is held in cash, which is not a risk factor and contributes no market risk.
explanation: A valid mapping preserves market value, so value not allocated to any risk factor is cash, which carries no market risk factor.
originalText: The remainder is held in cash, which is not a risk factor and so contributes no market risk.

statement: The choice of primitive risk factors in a VaR mapping reflects a trade-off between a better approximation of risk (more factors) and faster, simpler modelling (fewer factors).
explanation: More factors approximate portfolio risk better but make modelling more time consuming, while fewer factors are faster but leave more residual risk.
originalText: A trade‑off between a better approximation of risk (more factors) and faster, simpler modeling (fewer factors).

statement: Using as many risk factors as possible in a VaR mapping eliminates specific risk entirely.
explanation: More risk factors reduce specific risk but never eliminate it, and they raise modelling cost, which defeats the purpose of mapping.
originalText: The use of as many factors as possible, so that specific risk is eliminated entirely.

statement: In a VaR mapping, the amount of specific risk does not depend on which risk factors are chosen.
explanation: Specific risk is the residual left after the chosen general factors, so adding factors such as credit or currency reduces it.
originalText: The use of a single market factor, because specific risk does not depend on which factors are chosen.

statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve both the market value and the market risk of the position.
explanation: A valid mapping reproduces the position's current market value and also how that value responds to the risk factors.
originalText: The market value and the market risk of the position.

statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve only the market value of the position.
explanation: Matching value alone ignores risk, which is the purpose of mapping; the market risk must be preserved as well.
originalText: Only the market value of the position.
correction: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve both the market value and the market risk of the position.

changes.to: both the market value and the market risk

statement: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve the par value and the market risk of the position.
explanation: Par value is not the economic value of the position; the mapping preserves its market value.
originalText: The par value and the market risk of the position.
correction: Whichever approach is used to map a position onto risk factors, the mapping should preserve the market value and the market risk of the position.

changes.to: the market value

statement: A large equity portfolio is a good candidate for mapping because a small set of risk factors needs far fewer estimates than a full covariance matrix of all its positions.
explanation: The factor approach cuts the number of parameters to estimate dramatically compared with a covariance matrix of, say, 1,000 positions.
originalText: The large equity portfolio is a good candidate for mapping because a small set of general and specific factors needs far fewer estimates than a full covariance matrix of 1,000 positions.

statement: A corporate bond portfolio can be mapped to a small set of general risk factors, such as maturity vertices and rating spreads, rather than one factor per bond.
explanation: Fixed income positions are mapped to a limited set of general factors, not to one factor for each bond.
originalText: The corporate bond portfolio can be mapped to a small set of general risk factors, such as maturity vertices and rating spreads, rather than one factor per bond.

statement: Equity mapping contains model risk, including factor-sensitivity (beta) estimation error, subjective choice of risk factors, and omission of specific risk.
explanation: These are genuine sources of model risk in mapping equity positions to risk factors.
originalText: Equity mapping contains model risk, including factor‑sensitivity (beta) estimation error, subjective choice of risk factors, and omission of specific risk.

statement: Positions with little historical data, such as IPO funds and emergent assets, cannot be mapped to risk factors because their sensitivities cannot be estimated.
explanation: Lack of history is a reason to use mapping, not a barrier to it: such positions are expressed as exposures to similar risk factors that do have histories.
originalText: The IPO and emergent‑asset funds cannot be mapped because they lack historical data, so sensitivities cannot be estimated.

statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that a large portfolio has too many positions to model individually.
explanation: Too many positions make position-by-position computation impractical.
originalText: In a large portfolio there are too many positions to model individually.

statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that risk factors are common to various positions and/or instruments.
explanation: Common factors allow positions to be aggregated into a small set of exposures.
originalText: Risk factors are common to various positions and/or instruments.

statement: Mapping portfolio positions to risk factors allows for more accurate pricing (valuation) of the portfolio.
explanation: Mapping is a risk-measurement simplification, not a valuation tool; if anything it is less accurate than full valuation.
originalText: Risk factors allow for more accurate pricing (valuation) of the portfolio.

statement: One valid reason to map portfolio positions to risk factors is that it is typically easier to stress test the risk factors.
explanation: Stress scenarios are simpler to apply to a small set of risk factors than to every position.
originalText: It is typically easier to stress test the risk factors.

statement: Mapping aggregates risk exposures when it is impractical to treat each position separately.
explanation: This is a first principle of mapping: modelling each position separately would require too many computations.

statement: Mapping helps when there is insufficient price history for an investment, such as a recent IPO.
explanation: With no usable price history, mapping to risk factors replaces position-level history.

statement: Mapping helps with positions whose characteristics change over time, such as bonds that move toward maturity.
explanation: As a bond ages, its exposure is re-mapped to the relevant spot yields.

statement: Aggregating many positions into one risk factor is as acceptable for pricing a portfolio as it is for measuring its risk.
explanation: VaR mapping aggregates positions into common risk factors for risk measurement only; prices themselves cannot be aggregated.
correction: Aggregating many positions into one risk factor is acceptable for measuring a portfolio's risk but not for pricing it.

changes.from: is as acceptable for pricing a portfolio as it is for measuring its risk
changes.to: is acceptable for measuring a portfolio's risk but not for pricing it

statement: The market value of a commodity forward position is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
explanation: A position's market value is what gets allocated to risk factors; primitive risk factors are underlying market variables such as spot prices, FX rates and zero-coupon yields.
originalText: The market value of a commodity forward position

statement: The spot price of a commodity is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
explanation: Spot prices are standard primitive risk factors onto which position values are mapped.
originalText: The spot price of the commodity

statement: The spot foreign exchange rate is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
explanation: Spot FX rates are classic primitive risk factors.
originalText: The spot foreign exchange rate

statement: A zero-coupon yield is a primitive risk factor in a VaR mapping.
explanation: Zero-coupon yields are the primitive risk factors used for mapping fixed-income positions.
originalText: A zero‑coupon yield

statement: Measuring the current market value of each position is a step in the VaR mapping process.
explanation: Valuing the current positions is the first step.
originalText: Measure the current market value of each position.

statement: Allocating the market value of each position to one or more common risk factors is a step in the VaR mapping process.
explanation: Allocating each position to common factors is the core step of mapping.
originalText: Allocate the market value of each position to one or more common risk factors.

statement: Summing the allocated exposures across positions for each risk factor is a step in the VaR mapping process.
explanation: Summing by factor produces the vector of risk-factor exposures to which the factor distributions are applied.
originalText: Sum the allocated exposures across positions for each risk factor.

statement: Building a separate model from the full price history of every individual position is a step in the VaR mapping process.
explanation: Mapping works at the risk-factor level; modelling each position's own history is the position-by-position approach that mapping is designed to replace.
originalText: Build a separate model from the full price history of every individual position.

statement: Aggregating positions into risk factor exposures is acceptable for risk measurement even though prices themselves cannot be aggregated.
explanation: Risk measurement tolerates aggregation to risk factors, whereas pricing needs position-level precision.

statement: Pricing a portfolio may aggregate positions into a single risk factor, just as risk measurement does.
explanation: This reverses the principle: prices cannot be aggregated, although risk exposures can.

statement: VaR mapping is useful only when long price histories are available for each position.
explanation: Mapping is specifically useful when history is lacking, for example for recent IPOs.
originalText: Mapping is useful only when long price histories are available for each position.

statement: After mapping, the number of variables whose covariances must be estimated equals the number of positions.
explanation: Mapping reduces the number of variables to the number of risk factors, not the number of positions.
correction: After mapping, the number of variables whose covariances must be estimated equals the number of risk factors.

changes.to: equals the number of risk factors

statement: Mapping is the process of assigning risk factors to positions; in order to compute risk measures, risk factors have to be assigned to securities.
explanation: Mapping assigns each position's exposure to a set of risk factors so that risk measures can be computed.
originalText: Mapping is the process of assigning risk factors to positions; in order to compute risk measures, we have to assign risk factors to securities.

statement: When a position and its hedge can be mapped to the same risk factor or set of risk factors, the appropriate measure of value at risk is zero.
explanation: The mapped exposures offset exactly, but real basis, credit and idiosyncratic risk remain, so a VaR of zero is an artefact of the mapping rather than the true risk.
originalText: When the underlying position and its hedge can be mapped to the same risk factor (or set of risk factors), the appropriate measure of value at risk (VaR) is zero.

statement: Mapping decisions are often pragmatic: fixed-income cash-flow mappings are more accurate than duration mappings but are more complex and require more risk factors.
explanation: Cash-flow mapping uses many more vertices than a single-factor duration mapping, which gives more accuracy at the cost of complexity.
originalText: Mapping decisions are often pragmatic; for example, fixed‑income cash‑flow mappings are more accurate than duration mappings but are more complex and require more risk factors.

statement: As a practical matter, it may be difficult to find data that address certain risk factors, a problem that may merely mirror the real-world challenge of hedging or expressing some trade ideas.
explanation: Data availability limits which risk factors can be used.
originalText: As a practical matter, it may be difficult to find data that address certain risk factors, a problem that may merely mirror the real‑world challenge of hedging or expressing some trade ideas.

statement: In VaR mapping, a position's exposure to a primitive risk factor can be determined either analytically, as a partial derivative of the position value with respect to the risk factor, or empirically, as a regression slope estimated from historical returns.
explanation: Exposure is a sensitivity: it can be computed exactly from a valuation formula or estimated from data by regression, so both approaches are used.
originalText: Either analytically, as a partial derivative of the position value with respect to the risk factor, or empirically, as a regression slope estimated from historical returns.

statement: In VaR mapping, a position's exposure to a primitive risk factor can be determined only statistically, by regressing the position's returns on the risk factor's returns.
explanation: Regression is not the only way: for instruments with known pricing formulas the exposure is computed exactly as a partial derivative.
originalText: Only statistically, by regressing the position’s returns on the risk factor’s returns.

statement: In VaR mapping, a position's exposure to a primitive risk factor is set equal to the position's market value, regardless of how the value responds to the factor.
explanation: Exposure is a sensitivity; it equals market value only when the sensitivity is exactly one, for example a beta of 1.
originalText: By setting the exposure equal to the position’s market value, regardless of how the value responds to the factor.

statement: Principal component analysis of yield changes is the appropriate technique for reducing many highly correlated yield curve vertices to a few uncorrelated primitive risk factors such as level, slope and curvature.
explanation: PCA extracts a small number of uncorrelated components from correlated risk-factor changes, which suits dimension reduction in mapping.
originalText: Principal component analysis (PCA) of yield changes

statement: VaR mapping measures the current value of each position, replaces each with exposures to a small set of common risk factors (for example a proxy equity index for an IPO and standard-maturity interest rate vertices for bonds), and computes VaR from those exposures and the factors' covariance matrix.
explanation: Mapping simplifies the problem and handles positions with insufficient or irrelevant history, such as IPOs and aging bonds, through proxies.
originalText: Measure the current value of each position, replace each position with exposures to a small set of common risk factors (e.g., a proxy equity index for the IPO and standard‑maturity interest rate vertices for the bonds), and compute VaR from those exposures and the risk factors’ covariance matrix.

statement: VaR mapping is unsuitable for positions with limited price history, such as a recent IPO.
explanation: Mapping is precisely the tool for positions lacking sufficient history, because a proxy risk factor replaces the short return series.
originalText: Exclude the IPO from the VaR calculation until it has a full history, and map only the bonds because mapping is unsuitable for positions with limited data.

statement: Adding further general risk factors, such as credit spreads and currencies, to a mapping reduces the specific (residual) risk for a given total risk.
explanation: Specific risk is the residual left after the general factors, so the additional factors explain part of what was previously unexplained.
originalText: smaller, because the additional general factors explain part of what was previously unexplained.

statement: Adding further general risk factors to a mapping increases the specific (residual) risk for a given total risk, because more factors add more estimation error.
explanation: Extra factors move variance from the residual into the explained component, so specific risk falls rather than rises.
originalText: greater, because more factors add more estimation error.
correction: Adding further general risk factors to a mapping reduces the specific (residual) risk for a given total risk, because more factors add more estimation error.

changes.to: reduces

statement: Specific risk is unchanged when further general risk factors are added to a mapping, because it is independent of the choice of general factors.
explanation: Specific risk is defined as the residual after the chosen general factors, so it depends on which factors are used.
originalText: unchanged, because specific risk is independent of the choice of general factors.

statement: A stress test that shocks each zero-coupon vertex by its own VaR percentage does not use mapping to risk factors or the vertex VaRs, and is essentially a simulation that fully re-prices the component bonds.
explanation: Such a stress test is built directly from the mapped zero-coupon risk factors and their VaR percentages, not from an unmapped full re-pricing.
originalText: Because this stress test does not use mapping to risk factors, the VaRs of the zero‑coupon vertices are not used; it is essentially a simulation that fully re‑prices the component bonds.

statement: A stress test that shocks every zero-coupon vertex by its VaR at once gives a loss equal to the undiversified portfolio VaR, because it implicitly assumes all zeros are perfectly correlated.
explanation: Simultaneous VaR shocks to all zeros equal the sum of the vertex VaRs, which is the perfect-correlation case.
originalText: The stressed portfolio loss equals the undiversified portfolio VaR because the stress implicitly assumes all zeros are perfectly correlated.

statement: In a stress test that shocks zero-coupon vertices by their VaR percentages, the stressed loss increases if the confidence level and/or the yield volatility assumptions are increased.
explanation: Each zero's risk percentage is proportional to the confidence deviate and the yield volatility, so raising either enlarges the loss.
originalText: The stressed loss will increase if the confidence level is increased and/or the underlying yield volatility assumptions are increased.

statement: A forward contract to buy EUR against USD in one year can be mapped to a long EUR spot position, a long one-year EUR bill and a short one-year USD bill.
explanation: A forward decomposes into spot FX and two zero-coupon rate positions, which are elementary risk factors.
originalText: Mapping a long USD/EUR forward contract to a long EUR spot position, a long one‑year EUR bill and a short one‑year USD bill.

statement: Zero-coupon government bonds should be mapped to government bonds paying regular coupons.
explanation: The mapping runs the other way: a coupon bond is a portfolio of zero-coupon bonds, so coupon bonds are mapped onto zeros.
originalText: Mapping zero‑coupon government bonds to government bonds paying regular coupons.

statement: A position in a stock market index should be mapped to a position in one stock within that index.
explanation: Stocks are mapped onto the index (through beta); mapping the index onto one constituent introduces specific risk and loses diversification.
originalText: Mapping a position in a stock market index to a position in one stock within that index.

statement: In mapping a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, the fixed leg is equivalent to a coupon-paying bond and the floating leg to a floating-rate note.
explanation: The fixed leg has predetermined coupons like a fixed-coupon bond, while the floating leg's coupons reset to market so it behaves like a floating-rate note.
originalText: Fixed leg: coupon‑paying bond; floating leg: floating‑rate note

statement: In mapping a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, the fixed leg is equivalent to a floating-rate note and the floating leg to a coupon-paying bond.
explanation: The legs are reversed in this statement: the fixed leg is the coupon-paying bond and the floating leg is the floating-rate note.
originalText: Fixed leg: floating‑rate note; floating leg: coupon‑paying bond
correction: In mapping a plain-vanilla interest rate swap, the fixed leg is equivalent to a coupon-paying bond and the floating leg to a floating-rate note.

changes.from: the fixed leg is equivalent to a floating-rate note and the floating leg to a coupon-paying bond
changes.to: the fixed leg is equivalent to a coupon-paying bond and the floating leg to a floating-rate note

statement: An option portfolio mapped using a Taylor series approximation of the Black-Scholes-Merton price can be mapped to the spot price, volatility, interest rate, time to expiration and dividend yield.
explanation: The option value is differentiable in every BSM input, so the Taylor series gives sensitivities to spot, volatility, rate, time and dividend yield.
originalText: Spot price, volatility, interest rate, time to expiration, and dividend yield

statement: A short put option position loses value both when the underlying price falls and when implied volatility rises, because it has positive delta and negative vega.
explanation: A short put is long the underlying (positive delta) and short volatility (negative vega), so a price drop together with a volatility rise hurts on both.
originalText: Loss in value due to both risk factors

statement: A long call option loses value when the underlying price falls but gains value when implied volatility rises, so the delta loss is mitigated by the vega gain.
explanation: A long call has positive delta and positive vega, so a price decline reduces its value while a volatility rise increases it.
originalText: Loss in delta exposure mitigated by gain in vega exposure

statement: A forward currency position has three major risk factors: the spot price and two interest rates.
explanation: A currency forward maps to the spot FX rate and the domestic and foreign zero-coupon rates.
originalText: A forward currency position has three major risk factors: the spot price and two interest rates

statement: A forward rate agreement can be mapped to two risk factors: a long position in a zero-coupon bond (or bill) plus a short position in a zero-coupon bond (or bill).
explanation: An FRA is a long and a short zero-coupon position at the two relevant dates.
originalText: A forward rate agreement can be mapped to two risk factors: a long position in a zero‑coupon bond (or bill) plus a short position in a zero‑coupon bond (or bill)

statement: Because an interest rate swap is a bilateral contract, it cannot be effectively mapped to primitive risk factors, and simulation must be used to compute a diversified VaR.
explanation: A swap can be mapped to its cash-flow vertices (a fixed-coupon bond plus a floating-rate note), so the delta-normal approach gives a diversified VaR and simulation is not required.
originalText: Because an interest rate swap is a bilateral contract, it cannot be effectively mapped to primitive risk factors, and simulation must be used to compute a diversified VaR

statement: Near expiration, an at-the-money option becomes highly nonlinear in the underlying price, so a delta-only mapping is no longer adequate and gamma must be added as a risk factor.
explanation: Gamma rises sharply as an at-the-money option approaches expiry, so the second-order term is needed even over a one-day horizon.
originalText: She adds gamma as a risk factor because the first‑order linear approximation has become insufficient.

statement: The vega of an at-the-money option becomes larger as its time to expiration shortens.
explanation: Vega of an at-the-money option increases with maturity, so it shrinks as expiry nears.
originalText: She adds vega as a risk factor, which was omitted at long maturities but is more relevant at short maturities.
correction: The vega of an at-the-money option becomes smaller as its time to expiration shortens.

changes.from: becomes larger as its time to expiration shortens
changes.to: becomes smaller as its time to expiration shortens

statement: A stock option portfolio can be mapped in many ways, from simple (delta-normal) to complex (multiple Greek risk factors).
explanation: Options are nonlinear, so the mapping can range from a first-order delta approximation to multi-Greek approximations.
originalText: The stock option portfolio can be mapped in many ways, from simple (delta‑normal) to complex (multiple Greek risk factors).

statement: A forward foreign exchange contract is one of the most difficult instruments to map.
explanation: An FX forward maps cleanly into a spot position and two bill positions, making it among the easiest instruments to map.
originalText: The forward FX contract is one of the most difficult instruments to map.
correction: A forward foreign exchange contract is one of the easiest instruments to map.

changes.to: one of the easiest

statement: When mapping the risks of a foreign currency forward contract to risk factors, the volatility of the underlying spot exchange rate is the primary source of risk.
explanation: The forward's value tracks the spot rate adjusted for carry, and spot FX volatility is far larger than the price volatility of the short-term bills.
originalText: When mapping the risks of a foreign currency forward contract to risk factors, volatility of the underlying spot contract is the primary source of risk.

statement: Valuing a commodity forward through mapping is simpler and more precise than valuing a financial forward, since commodity forwards generally do not make periodic cash payments.
explanation: Convenience yield and storage costs are unobservable, so commodity forwards are harder and less precise to map than financial forwards.

statement: A key factor used in valuing a forward rate agreement is the convenience yield arising from the buyer's ability to lock in long-term borrowing rates.
explanation: Convenience yield is the benefit of holding a physical commodity; it is a commodity forward concept, not an FRA input.
originalText: A key factor used in valuing a forward rate agreement is the convenience yield arising from the buyer’s ability to lock in long‑term borrowing rates.

statement: A long 6x12 forward rate agreement is equivalent to a long 6-month bill and a short 12-month bill.
explanation: A sold FRA is short the 6-month bill and long the 12-month bill, and the long FRA is the mirror image, with every position reversed.
originalText: Long 6‑month bill and short 12‑month bill

statement: A long 6x12 forward rate agreement is equivalent to a short 6-month bill and a long 12-month bill.
explanation: That is the sold FRA (borrow for 6 months, invest for 12); the long FRA is long the 6-month bill and short the 12-month bill.
originalText: Short 6‑month bill and long 12‑month bill
correction: A long 6x12 forward rate agreement is equivalent to a long 6-month bill and a short 12-month bill.

changes.from: a short 6-month bill and a long 12-month bill
changes.to: a long 6-month bill and a short 12-month bill

statement: A forward contract to buy EUR for USD in one year decomposes into a long one-year EUR bill (with exposure to EUR spot) and a short one-year USD bill.
explanation: A long forward replicates buying the foreign bill, financed by borrowing the domestic bill.
originalText: Long a one‑year EUR bill (with exposure to EUR spot) and short a one‑year USD bill with face value USD 126.5 million

statement: A forward contract to buy EUR for USD in one year decomposes into a short one-year EUR bill and a long one-year USD bill.
explanation: The signs are reversed: this replicates a forward to sell euros, whereas buying euros forward is long the EUR bill and short the USD bill.
originalText: Short a one‑year EUR bill and long a one‑year USD bill with face value USD 126.5 million
correction: A forward contract to buy EUR for USD in one year decomposes into a long one-year EUR bill and a short one-year USD bill.

changes.from: a short one-year EUR bill and a long one-year USD bill
changes.to: a long one-year EUR bill and a short one-year USD bill

statement: The interest rate legs of a currency forward can be ignored in VaR mapping because they are riskless.
explanation: The bill legs have small but non-zero price risk and are part of the mapping of a currency forward.
originalText: Long EUR spot only; the interest rate legs are ignored because they are riskless

statement: A 5-year currency swap with annual exchanges is equivalent to a single forward contract maturing in 5 years.
explanation: A single forward captures only one exchange date; the swap is a portfolio of forwards, one for each payment date.
originalText: It is equivalent to a single forward contract maturing in 5 years.

statement: A currency swap is not equivalent to a portfolio of forward contracts, because a swap has a non-zero value at initiation.
explanation: A swap is normally priced to have zero value at initiation, and its equivalence to a portfolio of forwards does not depend on that.
originalText: It is not equivalent to a portfolio of forward contracts, because a swap has a non‑zero value at initiation.

statement: The most likely risk factors for a foreign currency forward contract in VaR mapping are the spot exchange rate, the domestic interest rate and the foreign interest rate.
explanation: A currency forward is priced off spot FX and the two interest rates, so these three drive its value.
originalText: Spot exchange rate, domestic interest rate, and foreign interest rate

statement: The most likely risk factors for a foreign currency forward contract in VaR mapping are the convenience yield, the domestic interest rate and the foreign interest rate.
explanation: Convenience yield is a commodity factor and is not relevant to currency forwards.
originalText: Convenience yield, domestic interest rate, and foreign interest rate

statement: The most likely risk factors for a foreign currency forward contract in VaR mapping are the spot exchange rate, the foreign interest rate and storage cost.
explanation: Storage cost is a commodity feature and is irrelevant for currency forwards; the domestic interest rate is the missing factor.
originalText: Spot exchange rate, foreign interest rate, and storage cost

statement: Mapping a commodity forward is harder than mapping a currency forward because commodity forward prices embed a convenience yield, which is highly variable and not tied to another observable financial variable.
explanation: Convenience yield is an additional, unobservable and highly variable risk factor with no financial-market counterpart.
originalText: Commodity forward prices embed a convenience yield, which is highly variable and not tied to another observable financial variable.

statement: Commodity forwards cannot be expressed as a combination of spot and bond positions.
explanation: Commodity forwards can still be decomposed into spot and zero-coupon positions; the difficulty lies in the extra convenience yield factor.

statement: Commodity forwards have no sensitivity to domestic interest rates.
explanation: Commodity forwards are still sensitive to the interest rate through the cost of carry.

statement: Commodity spot prices cannot be observed, whereas FX spot rates can.
explanation: Commodity spot prices are observable; the difficulty in mapping commodity forwards is the convenience yield.

statement: A 5-year currency swap with annual exchanges is equivalent to a portfolio of 5 forward contracts, one for each annual exchange date, each mapped to its own risk factors.
explanation: A swap is a portfolio of forwards with one forward per exchange date, so mapping the swap means mapping each of those forwards.
originalText: It is equivalent to a portfolio of 5 forward contracts, one for each annual exchange date, each mapped to its own risk factors.

statement: A currency swap cannot be represented by forward contracts because it has multiple payment dates.
explanation: Multiple payment dates are the reason a swap is decomposed into several forwards, not a barrier to doing so.
originalText: It cannot be represented by forward contracts because a swap has multiple payment dates.
correction: A currency swap can be represented by a portfolio of forward contracts because it has multiple payment dates.

changes.from: cannot be represented by forward contracts because it has
changes.to: can be represented by a portfolio of forward contracts because it has

statement: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually equal to the maturity of the CDO.
explanation: The Gaussian copula fixes one default correlation over the whole life of the CDO, so its measurement horizon is the CDO's maturity.
originalText: the maturity of the CDO.

statement: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually equal to the reinvestment period of the CDO.
explanation: The reinvestment period is only the phase during which proceeds are reinvested; it does not define the horizon of the default correlation.
originalText: the reinvestment period of the CDO.
correction: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually equal to the maturity of the CDO.

changes.to: the maturity

statement: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually equal to the time until the first asset in the CDO defaults.
explanation: The time to first default is an outcome the model describes, not the horizon over which the correlation is measured.
originalText: the time until the first asset in the CDO defaults.
correction: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually equal to the maturity of the CDO.

changes.from: the time until the first asset in the CDO defaults
changes.to: the maturity of the CDO

statement: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually a one-day horizon, as in a standard VaR calculation.
explanation: A one-day horizon is typical of VaR-style time-series work, not of a copula spanning the CDO's life.
originalText: a one‑day horizon, as in a standard VaR calculation.
correction: The original copula approach for a CDO is a static financial correlation measure whose single fixed time period is usually the maturity of the CDO.

changes.from: a one-day horizon, as in a standard VaR calculation
changes.to: the maturity of the CDO

statement: When the correlation between two assets is negative, if one asset's value decreases the other asset's value on average increases, which reduces overall risk.
explanation: Opposite co-movement means gains and losses offset, so combining the assets lowers portfolio risk.
originalText: If one asset’s value decreases, the other asset’s value on average increases, which reduces overall risk.

statement: When the correlation between two assets is negative, if one asset's value decreases the other asset's value on average also decreases, which reduces overall risk.
explanation: Assets that fall together describe positive correlation, which would not reduce risk; with negative correlation the other asset tends to rise.
originalText: If one asset’s value decreases, the other asset’s value on average also decreases, which reduces overall risk.
correction: When the correlation between two assets is negative, if one asset's value decreases the other asset's value on average increases, which reduces overall risk.

changes.to: increases

statement: When the correlation between two assets is negative, if one asset's value decreases the other asset's value on average increases, which increases overall risk.
explanation: The direction is right but the conclusion is wrong: offsetting moves reduce, not increase, overall risk.
originalText: If one asset’s value decreases, the other asset’s value on average increases, which increases overall risk.
correction: When the correlation between two assets is negative, if one asset's value decreases the other asset's value on average increases, which reduces overall risk.

changes.to: which reduces overall risk

statement: When the correlation between two assets is negative, the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of the two assets is greater than the average of the two stand-alone standard deviations.
explanation: With correlation below 1, portfolio volatility is below the weighted average of the stand-alone volatilities, and lower still when correlation is negative.
originalText: The standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of the two assets is greater than the average of the two stand‑alone standard deviations.
correction: When the correlation between two assets is negative, the standard deviation of an equally weighted portfolio of the two assets is less than the average of the two stand-alone standard deviations.

changes.to: less than

statement: Correlation trading refers to trading assets whose prices are determined by the co-movement of two or more assets over time.
explanation: Correlation trading means taking positions, such as multi-asset options or correlation swaps, whose value is driven by how assets move together.
originalText: trading assets whose prices are determined by the co‑movement of two or more assets over time.

statement: Correlation trading refers to trading each asset only on the basis of its own stand-alone market and economic conditions.
explanation: That describes single-asset trading; correlation trading depends on the co-movement of assets.
originalText: trading each asset only on the basis of its own stand‑alone market and economic conditions.

statement: Correlation trading refers to trading only assets that are uncorrelated, to eliminate correlation risk.
explanation: Avoiding correlated assets is risk avoidance, not correlation trading.
originalText: trading only assets that are uncorrelated, to eliminate correlation risk.

statement: Correlation trading refers to trading assets whose prices depend only on the individual volatility of a single underlying asset.
explanation: Single-asset volatility trading is not correlation trading; the payoff must depend on joint movement of assets.
originalText: trading assets whose prices depend only on the individual volatility of a single underlying asset.

statement: A non-zero Pearson correlation between two variables implies that the variables are dependent.
explanation: Independence implies zero correlation, so a non-zero correlation rules out independence.
originalText: As the correlation is non‑zero, we can say there is a dependency between the variables; for example, we can say ”the variables are dependent”.

statement: If the covariance between two variables stays fixed and positive, an increase in the standard deviation of one of the variables lowers their correlation.
explanation: The standard deviations are in the denominator of the correlation coefficient, which equals the covariance divided by their product.
originalText: If the covariance does not change, an increase in the standard deviation (volatility) of one of the variables will decrease the correlation to a value below 0.20.

statement: The CDS spread is a continuously increasing function of the default correlation between the CDS seller and the reference asset.
explanation: Because of wrong-way risk, the CDS spread decreases as the default correlation between seller and reference asset rises.
originalText: If the correlation is a default correlation between a credit default swap (CDS) seller and the reference asset, the correlation must be monotonically increasing; i.e., the CDS spread is a continuously increasing function of a higher default correlation.
correction: The CDS spread is a decreasing function of the default correlation between the CDS seller and the reference asset.

changes.to: a decreasing function

statement: The term correlation is uniquely defined.
explanation: Correlation has no single unique definition; it is used loosely for Pearson correlation and other measures of co-movement.
originalText: The term ”correlation” is uniquely defined.

statement: Measures of association or measures of dependence refer to the linear Pearson correlation coefficient.
explanation: Measures of association or dependence are broader than, and typically not limited to, the Pearson correlation coefficient.

statement: Concentration risk has the same mathematical definition as correlation risk.
explanation: Concentration risk and correlation risk are related, because the concentration ratio moves with default correlation, but they are not the same quantity.

statement: In trading practice, such as on correlation desks or in correlation trading, the term correlation is defined broadly and can refer to any co-movement of assets over time.
explanation: In practice correlation is a broad term covering any co-movement of assets over time, not one unique measure.
originalText: In trading practice (e.g. correlation desks or correlation trading), the term correlation is defined broadly and can refer to any co‑movement of assets over time.

statement: Wrong-way risk is a type of (special case of) correlation risk.
explanation: Wrong-way risk arises from positive correlation between exposure and counterparty default, which is a form of correlation risk.
originalText: Wrong‑way risk is a type of (special case of) correlation risk.

statement: Statistical independence between two variables implies that their Pearson correlation coefficient is zero.
explanation: Independence implies zero covariance and hence zero correlation, although zero correlation does not imply independence.
originalText: Statistical independence between two variables implies their Pearson correlation coefficient is zero.

statement: Correlation risk only refers to financial variables and excludes non-financial variables, such as economic or geopolitical events, because they are impossible to parameterize.
explanation: The definition of correlation risk explicitly includes non-financial variables such as GDP or political events.
originalText: Correlation risk only refers to financial variables and excludes non‑financial variables (e.g. economic or geopolitical events) because they are impossible to parameterize.

statement: A creditor's worst-case scenario is reduced by a lower concentration ratio and/or a lower default correlation.
explanation: Both a lower concentration ratio and a lower default correlation reduce the worst-case joint default probability.
originalText: A creditor’s worst‑case scenario is reduced by either a lower concentration ratio and/or a lower default correlation.

statement: The buyer of a CDS faces wrong-way risk when there is a positive default correlation between the reference asset and the CDS seller.
explanation: The seller is then likely to default exactly when protection is needed.
originalText: The buyer of a CDS faces wrong‑way risk when there is a positive default correlation between the reference asset and the CDS counterparty.

statement: The risk-adjusted return of a portfolio typically increases when the correlations of the assets in the portfolio increase.
explanation: Higher correlations reduce diversification, raising portfolio volatility and lowering the return-to-risk ratio.
originalText: The risk‑adjusted return of a portfolio typically increases when correlations of assets in the portfolio increase.
correction: The risk-adjusted return of a portfolio typically decreases when the correlations of the assets in the portfolio increase.

changes.to: decreases

statement: Dynamic correlation risk in a portfolio of pairs trades is most appropriately estimated using Gaussian copulas.
explanation: A Gaussian copula is a static correlation tool and does not capture dynamic correlation in pairs trades.

statement: Correlation risk is highest during periods of relatively benign market movements, when correlations are difficult to predict.
explanation: Correlation risk peaks in stressed markets, such as 2007-09, when correlations jump toward one.
originalText: Correlation risk is highest during periods of relatively benign market movements when correlations are difficult to predict.

statement: Pairs trading is an example of a dynamic financial correlation measure.
explanation: Pairs trading exploits how the co-movement of two assets evolves through time, so it is a dynamic correlation application.
originalText: Pairs trading.

statement: The binomial default correlation model is an example of a dynamic financial correlation measure.
explanation: The binomial default correlation model is static: it measures one-period default dependence.
originalText: Binomial default correlation model.
correction: The binomial default correlation model is an example of a static financial correlation measure.

changes.from: an example of a dynamic financial correlation measure
changes.to: an example of a static financial correlation measure

statement: Copula correlations for collateralized debt obligations are an example of a dynamic financial correlation measure.
explanation: CDO copula correlations are static, because the copula takes a fixed correlation input.
originalText: Copula correlations for collateralized debt obligations (CDOs).
correction: Copula correlations for collateralized debt obligations are an example of a static financial correlation measure.

changes.from: an example of a dynamic financial correlation measure
changes.to: an example of a static financial correlation measure
